evidence.claim: Route 68 heads inland from Highway 1 near the Monterey County Fairgrounds, passing Monterey Regional Airport and the junction for Del Rey Oaks.
evidence.quote: SR 68 exits SR 1 as the Monterey-Salinas Highway, which is a freeway for the first half mile. The freeway becomes a highway and passes by the Monterey Regional Airport, intersecting SR 218 at Del Rey Oaks

evidence.claim: Caltrans designates the section from Highway 1 to the Salinas River as scenic.
evidence.quote: only the part from SR 1 to the Salinas River is designated by Caltrans as a scenic highway.

evidence.claim: That 14-mile stretch offers views of chaparral and springtime lupine, the landscape features behind its scenic status.
evidence.quote: The Monterey-Salinas Highway is a California Scenic Route because of its views of the chaparral and springtime lupin for 14 miles (23 km) between State Route 1 in Monterey to the Salinas River.

evidence.claim: In 1937, a dirt wagon road became a paved two-lane highway.
evidence.quote: Highway 68 was upgraded from a dirt wagon road to a 2-lane paved road in 1937.

evidence.claim: Caltrans planned a freeway between Monterey and Salinas during the 1950s and 1960s, but environmental concerns ended that plan. Only short sections were built.
evidence.quote: During the 1950s and 1960s, Caltrans had planned to upgrade Highway 68 to a freeway between Salinas and Highway 1 in Monterey

evidence.claim: The Spreckels section opened in 1967 with two new Salinas River bridges, replacing an 1889 truss bridge.
evidence.quote: The segment around Spreckels opened in 1967 and included a pair of new bridges spanning the Salinas River, which replaced an old truss bridge built in 1889.

evidence.claim: but environmental concerns ended that plan. Only short sections were built.
evidence.quote: The freeway plan died as a result of environmental concerns along the route. The only portions of this freeway that were actually built were a 1-mile (1.6 km) section approaching the Highway 1 interchange in Monterey, and a 3-mile (4.8 km) segment starting in Spreckels and heading west

evidence.claim: Driving east from Monterey, the route passes Laguna Seca, then Laureles Grade, Corral de Tierra and San Benancio before Toro Park and Spreckels.
evidence.quote: The route goes past Pasadera, WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca, Laureles Grade, Corral De Tierra, San Benancio, Toro Park and Spreckels

evidence.claim: The Salinas River marks the end of the designated scenery; the numbered highway continues into Salinas, becoming South Main Street and then following John Street to U.S. 101.
evidence.quote: At the city limits, SR 68 becomes South Main Street and continues to downtown. SR 68 makes a right off of Main and follows John Street to its terminus at U.S. Route 101.

evidence.claim: Laguna Seca’s circuit was laid out around a dry lake bed, which gave the track its Spanish name.
evidence.quote: The name Laguna Seca is Spanish for dry lake:  the area where the track now lies was once a lake, and the course was built around the dry lake bed.

evidence.claim: Local businesses and individuals raised $1.5 million to build it in 1957 on part of the Army’s Fort Ord, after the Pebble Beach Road Races were abandoned as too dangerous.
evidence.quote: The track was built in 1957 at a cost of $1.5 million raised from local businesses and individuals on part of the US Army's Fort Ord (a maneuver area and field artillery target range) after the nearby Pebble Beach Road Races were abandoned for being too dangerous.

evidence.claim: Architect Wallace Holm marked the course in the dirt and walked its line for the bulldozers.
evidence.quote: When the bulldozers came in, he drew the path out on the dirt, and then walked around in a circle to show them where to go.

evidence.claim: The circuit has since changed, but its Corkscrew combines a blind approach with a 59-foot drop.
evidence.quote: due to the 59 ft (18 m) drop in elevation as well as its blind crest and apex on the uphill approach.

evidence.claim: Architect Wallace Holm
evidence.quote: The lead designer of the track was the young architect Wallace Holm

evidence.claim: The circuit has since changed
evidence.quote: The track itself has undergone significant changes over the past two decades

evidence.claim: Castle Rock gave Corral de Tierra its name: a fence of earth. John Steinbeck and his sister Mary played at its base as children.
evidence.quote: In their youth, Steinbeck and his sister, Mary, played at the base of Castle Rock, the "fence of earth" giving Corral de Tierra its Spanish name.

evidence.claim: Steinbeck later set The Pastures of Heaven, his 1932 cycle of short stories, in the valley.
evidence.quote: John Steinbeck’s The Pastures of Heaven, a short story cycle published in 1932, is set in the valley.

evidence.claim: The community lies along Highway 68 between Salinas and the Monterey Peninsula, on land formerly within Rancho Corral de Tierra.
evidence.quote: It is located in the Corral de Tierra Valley, on the former land grant of Rancho Corral de Tierra

evidence.claim: The community lies along Highway 68 between Salinas and the Monterey Peninsula
evidence.quote: The community of Corral de Tierra lies along Highway 68 midway between Salinas and the Monterey Peninsula.

evidence.claim: Spreckels was built to house sugar-factory workers. The Spreckels Sugar Company plant operated here from 1899 to 1982, processing beets on an industrial scale.
evidence.quote: It was built to house workers for the Spreckels Sugar Company plant, which operated there from 1899 until 1982

evidence.claim: When it opened, it consumed 13 million U.S. gallons of water a day to process 3,000 short tons of beets, with much of that water pumped from wells.
evidence.quote: each day consuming 13,000,000 US gal (49,000,000 L) of water—with much of it pumped from wells—to process 3,000 short tons (2,700 t) of beets.

evidence.claim: The company began selling houses to the public in about 1925, loosening its control of the town. John Steinbeck lived and worked here for a time.
evidence.quote: The company began to relinquish control of the town when they started selling homes in the community to the public in about 1925.

evidence.claim: John Steinbeck lived and worked here for a time.
evidence.quote: Spreckels is associated with the writer John Steinbeck, who lived and worked there for a time

evidence.claim: The Monterey-Salinas Highway begins with a freeway section before continuing past the airport toward the inland communities. It is one part of the longer SR 68, which runs from Pacific Grove to Salinas.
evidence.quote: It runs from Asilomar State Beach in Pacific Grove to U.S. Route 101 in Salinas.

evidence.claim: The built eastern segment bypassed Toro Park, leaving a three-mile fragment of the larger scheme.
evidence.quote: a 3-mile (4.8 km) segment starting in Spreckels and heading west, bypassing the unincorporated village of Toro Park.

evidence.claim: In 1974, the property passed to the Monterey County Parks Department and became part of its park system.
evidence.quote: In 1974 the property was deeded over to the Monterey County Parks Department and continues to be part of the park system.

evidence.claim: The neighboring San Benancio Canyon also appears in the landscape behind Steinbeck’s stories. Its slopes carry California live oaks, wild sage brush and grass, while Toro Creek runs beside the canyon walls.
evidence.quote: The walls of San Benancio Canyon have an elevation of 400 ft and run adjacent to Toro Creek, a small tributary to the Salinas River which is located four miles south. The canyon is home to a number of California Live Oak Trees and various types of wild sage brush and grass.

evidence.claim: The neighboring San Benancio Canyon also appears in the landscape behind Steinbeck’s stories.
evidence.quote: San Benancio was the inspiration for "Las Pasturas del Cielo," the fictional setting in John Steinbeck’s Pastures of Heaven.

evidence.claim: south of Salinas.

evidence.quote: SR 68 is concurrent with SR 1 for 2.5 miles (4.0 km) until nearing the Monterey County Fairgrounds. At this point, SR 68 exits SR 1 as the Monterey-Salinas Highway
